title: The infinitive: forms

objectives.can: Recognise infinitives of every tense and voice and name them.

explanation.summary: The infinitive is a verb form with no person, number or mood. It has tense and voice like other verbs, and it behaves like a neuter noun. This lesson teaches its forms; the many ways it is used come in Stage 5.

sections.heading: What an infinitive is
body: A finite verb tells you who acts and how the speaker puts the action: person, number, mood. An infinitive does neither. It names an action: λέγειν, 'to say' or 'saying'; ἔχειν, 'to have'. It has a tense stem and a voice, so you can say 'present active infinitive' or 'aorist passive infinitive', but it has no ending for person or number. It never changes for them.

In Philippians 1:21 two infinitives are used like nouns, each with a neuter article in front: τὸ ζῆν and τὸ ἀποθανεῖν, 'living' and 'dying'. In Mark 10:45 three infinitives follow the verb ἦλθεν and say what the Son of Man did not come to do and what he did come to do. Both uses belong to Stage 5. What matters here is how to see that a word is an infinitive and which tense and voice it has.

sections.heading: The endings
body: Almost every infinitive ends in -ναι, -σαι, -σθαι, -ειν or -εῖν (or in a contracted -ᾶν or -οῦν). The ending shows the tense and voice together. The present active adds -ειν to the present stem: λέγειν, ἔχειν, ἀκούειν. Contract verbs contract it: ποιεῖν, λαλεῖν, ἀγαπᾶν, πληροῦν. The present middle and passive ends in -εσθαι: πορεύεσθαι, ἔρχεσθαι.

The first aorist active ends in -σαι with no augment: ποιῆσαι, λῦσαι, πιστεῦσαι. The first aorist middle ends in -σασθαι: προσεύξασθαι, εὐαγγελίσασθαι. The aorist passive ends in -θῆναι: σωθῆναι, βαπτισθῆναι, διακονηθῆναι. The second aorist, built on the aorist stem, ends in -εῖν in the active (ἐλθεῖν, ἰδεῖν, φαγεῖν, ἀποθανεῖν) and in -έσθαι in the middle (γενέσθαι).

The perfect active ends in -κέναι: γεγονέναι, ἑστάναι, and the irregular εἰδέναι. The perfect middle and passive ends in -σθαι, added to the perfect stem with its reduplication: πεφανερῶσθαι, κατηρτίσθαι, οἰκοδομῆσθαι. The future infinitive exists but is rare: ἔσεσθαι, 'to be' as something still to come, is the commonest. Verbs in -μι and εἰμί have -ναι: εἶναι, διδόναι (present), δοῦναι (aorist), ἀφιέναι, θεῖναι, στῆναι.

sections.heading: Present or aorist? Aspect, not time
body: The infinitive itself does not say when the action takes place. The tense stem shows the aspect, as in the other moods outside the indicative. A present infinitive sees the action as going on, repeated or in general; an aorist infinitive sees it as a whole. In Acts 20:35 μακάριόν ἐστιν μᾶλλον διδόναι ἢ λαμβάνειν puts two present infinitives side by side: giving and receiving, taken as practices. In Philippians 1:21 τὸ ζῆν is present, 'life as it goes on', and τὸ ἀποθανεῖν is aorist, 'the event of dying'. The perfect infinitive views a state that results: πεφανερῶσθαι in Hebrews 9:8 is 'to have been made known and to stand revealed'.

When the time of the action matters, the main verb and the context tell you. An infinitive after a verb of saying may refer to an earlier event, one after ἔδει to what must happen, and so on. Stage 5 returns to this.

sections.heading: Where learners go wrong
body: Three endings need care. First, -εῖν is the ending of two different forms: the contract present active (ποιεῖν, λαλεῖν) and the second aorist active (ἐλθεῖν, ἰδεῖν). The spelling is the same. You must know the verb: ποιέω and λαλέω have a present stem in -ε-, while ἔρχομαι and ὁράω take their aorist from a different stem (ἐλθ-, ἰδ-).

Second, -σαι at the end of a word is the first aorist active infinitive, but it is also the ending of an optative third person singular (ἁγιάσαι) and of the aorist middle imperative second person singular. The sentence decides, and you met this in the lesson on the optative.
Third, -σθαι and -εσθαι cover middle and passive together in the present and the perfect. As with other forms you decide between middle and passive from the verb and the context.

misunderstandings: Looking for a subject ending on an infinitive. It has none; its subject is in the sentence and, if named, is usually in the accusative.
Treating the aorist infinitive as a past infinitive. It has no augment and no past time; it shows the aspect of a whole action.
Thinking every -ειν is present. ἐλθεῖν, ἰδεῖν and φαγεῖν are second aorist forms, and the aspect is aorist.
Confusing -σαι (infinitive) with the optative or the aorist imperative: the sentence settles which.

deeper.heading: The infinitive as a frozen case
body: Historically the infinitive began as a noun, a case form of a verbal noun, and it then became attached to the verb system. This is why the endings -ναι and -σθαι do not look like the endings of other verb forms, and why the infinitive can stand with an article as a neuter noun: τὸ ζῆν. The whole development lies before the New Testament, and for reading it is enough to treat the infinitive as a verb form with a noun's habits.
